experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis is feasible given the compute and data constraints. The MoleculeNet ESOL dataset is available and contains the necessary SMILES representations and measured solubility values. Both GNN and fingerprint-based models can be implemented within the parameter budget constraint using standard libraries like PyTorch Geometric and scikit-learn. The experiment can be run on a single GPU node with typical SLURM scheduling.
experiment_plans.objective: To determine whether a Graph Neural Network (GNN) model using SMILES representations and attention mechanisms achieves statistically significant higher predictive accuracy for compound solubility compared to a fingerprint-based model with an equal number of trainable parameters, as measured by RMSE on the MoleculeNet ESOL dataset.
experiment_plans.design: Comparative benchmark experiment with two treatment groups: GNN model with attention mechanisms and fingerprint-based model, each constrained to have equal trainable parameters. The models are trained and evaluated on the same dataset split to ensure fair comparison.

data_requirements.description: The MoleculeNet ESOL dataset provides real-world measured solubility values and SMILES representations suitable for both model types. It contains 1128 compounds with measured log solubility in mols per litre and SMILES strings for molecular structure representation.
preprocessing_steps: Load the CSV file using pandas.read_csv()
Extract SMILES strings and measured log solubility values
Split data into train/validation/test sets (80/10/10) using stratified sampling
Convert SMILES to molecular graphs for GNN model using RDKit
Generate molecular fingerprints for fingerprint-based model using RDKit Morgan fingerprints
Normalize the target variable (measured log solubility) to zero mean and unit variance

methods.name: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)
methods.description: A GNN model using SMILES representations and attention mechanisms to predict compound solubility. The model processes molecular structures as graphs with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, applying message passing and attention mechanisms to learn molecular features.

methods.name: Molecular Fingerprints
methods.description: A fingerprint-based model using Morgan fingerprints as input features to predict compound solubility. This serves as the baseline model for comparison with the GNN approach.

methods.name: Attention Mechanisms
methods.description: Attention mechanisms integrated into the GNN model to improve interpretability and performance by focusing on relevant parts of the molecular graph during prediction.

methods.name: SMILES Representation
methods.description: SMILES strings are used as the primary input format for the GNN model, converting molecular structures into a format suitable for graph-based processing.

evaluation.baseline: The fingerprint-based model with equal number of trainable parameters
evaluation.success_criteria: If the GNN model achieves a lower RMSE than the fingerprint-based model, supporting the hypothesis. If the RMSE values are not significantly different, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Load moleculenet_esol_delaney_solubility.csv and extract SMILES strings and measured log solubility values. Split into train/validation/test sets (80/10/10) using stratified sampling.
Preprocess SMILES strings into molecular graphs using RDKit for the GNN model. Generate Morgan fingerprints for the fingerprint-based model.
Implement a GNN model with attention mechanisms using PyTorch Geometric. Configure the model architecture to match the parameter count of the fingerprint-based model.
Implement a fingerprint-based model using scikit-learn's Random Forest or similar algorithm. Ensure both models have approximately equal trainable parameters.
Train both models on the training set with the same validation set for hyperparameter tuning. Use early stopping based on validation loss.
Evaluate both models on the test set and calculate RMSE for each model.
Perform statistical significance testing (paired t-test) between the RMSE values of the two models to determine if the difference is significant.

risks: Parameter count mismatch between models due to different architectures
Overfitting in either model due to limited dataset size (1128 samples)
Computational time exceeding SLURM allocation limits for model training
Inconsistent preprocessing steps affecting model performance comparison
